name: Dormalex
description: A fast-acting GABAergic compound engineered to override BCI ping-response loops and force full cortical shutdown within 25-35 seconds of administration. Dormalex temporarily severs the handshake between the user's neural interface and their sleep architecture, allowing genuine unconsciousness regardless of active alerts or background processes. The resulting sleep is clean and uninterrupted for a user-defined window of 4-8 hours.
effects: No grogginess on wake cycle if timed correctly
side_effects: Missed emergency alerts during sleep window
Occasional hypnic jerk cascade on onset
Mild retrograde memory fog for 10-15 minutes post-wake
Dependency develops with nightly use within 3 weeks
cultural_context: Dormalex is the working person's survival drug. Tier 2 shift workers, warehouse operators, and transit runners who can't afford to lie awake staring at their BCI overlay at 3am are the core market. There's no stigma — using it is considered practical, almost responsible. The problem is that once you start, sleeping without it feels impossible.
story_hooks: A user's BCI was supposed to suppress alerts during their Dormalex window — but someone overrode the suppression remotely and pinged them with a kill order they never received, leading to a hit that went wrong.
A Tier 2 worker discovers they've been dreaming the same structured sequence every night on Dormalex — too structured to be random. Someone is feeding content into the gap the drug creates.
